newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Militia leader trial to open at Rwanda tribunal.
newsitem.headline: Militia leader trial to open at Rwanda tribunal.

text.p: The International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda starts its second trial on Tuesday when former Hutu militia leader Georges Rutaganda faces charges of genocide and crimes against humanity.
Rutaganda's trial is expected to start at 9.30 A.M. (0630 GMT) and follows that of former mayor Jean-Paul Akayesu.

Rutaganda, 39 and a Rwandan Hutu, was vice-president of the extremist Interahamwe militia held responsible for massacres during the 1994 genocide of an estimated 800,000 ethnic Tutsis and politically-moderate Hutus.
Under the rules of the U.N.'s Rwanda tribunal, Rutaganda faces life imprisonment if found guilty. His defence team comprises Luc De Temmerman of Belgium and Canadian Tiphaine Dickson.
He has been held in Arusha, the northern Tanzanian town where the tribunal sits, since his extradition from Zambia last May.
U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan dismissed two top tribunal officials last month after a U.N. report detailed administrative mismanagement, unqualified staff and legal chaos.

Rutaganda, a former agricultural engineer and businessman, was charged last May with eight counts of genocide, crimes against humanity (extermination), crimes against humanity (murder) and violations of Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions.
His trial was adjourned to Tuesday.
The trial of Jean-Paul Akayesu which began on January 9 has been suspended until May 12 to give time for the defence to prepare after the prosecution completed its case.
The Rwanda tribunal has so far indicted 21 people.

Rutaganda is accused of arming Hutu extremists in April 1994 and ordering the murder of Tutsi civilians with machetes, guns, grenades and drowning. The prosecution alleges that some victims were forced to dig their own graves.
Rutaganda is also charged with distributing weapons to Interahamwe militia and stationing militiamen near his office in the Rwandan capital Kigali to catch ethnic minority Tutsis.
He is charged with taking part in an attack on a technical school where thousands of unarmed Tutsi men, women and children were sheltering and in a follow-up attack on survivors.
The six-page indictment says in June 1994 Rutaganda ordered people to bury the bodies of victims to conceal their crimes.

The killings broke out in the tiny central African country after the assassination of Hutu president Juvenal Habyarimana on April 6 1994. Angry followers including the army, militia and Hutu civilians hunted down Tutsis -- blamed for Habyarimana's death -- and Hutus opposed to the military rule.

In Rwanda itself, where the death penalty exists for the most guilty, there are up to 90,000 detainees waiting to be charged, tried or released by the local justice system. Eleven people have so far received the death penalty while 16 have been sentenced to life imprisonment.
